name: Duvle
confidence_why: 2 sources read support the record, but its own quotation is not confirmed first-hand
catalog_citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-85), 133-236. Canberra: Australian National University. [Duvle phonology relayed from Murdoch, Charlotte, n.d.1, Duvle phonology summary, unpublished ms, SIL Jayapura -- not seen]
catalog_locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology', p.152 (PDF p.20); Appendix 3 intro, p.160 (PDF p.28); sec. 6 'The Duvle isolate', p.143 (PDF p.11). File: the copy we hold (symlink to), text checked with during this reading.
catalog_quote: [p.152] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours) ... [p.160] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. [p.143] There is very limited data on the phonology of Duvle. What is available is in the form of a summary, which does not include examples.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Duvle is a tone language with a two-way (high vs low) lexical tone contrast; stress has not been found contrastive in any Lakes Plain language (family-level remark). No source states where (non-contrastive) stress falls in Duvle.
new_statements.exceptions: none; Clouse notes his Duvle information rests on Murdoch's unpublished phonology summary without examples
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statement is Duvle-specific but second-hand (from Murdoch n.d. 'Duvle phonology summary'); the stress remark is a family-wide generalisation in the word-list appendix, not a Duvle-specific placement rule. The first-syllable stress sentence in McAllister & McAllister 1991 p.133 belongs to neighbouring Doutai, not Duvle.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1997's Duvle data are Murdoch's, from Dagai village (Eastern Duvle dialect per Ethnologue's Eastern/Western split); glottocode duvl1242 (not the Duvle-Wano pidgin duvl1238). The first-syllable stress statement found via Google Books (Workpapers 9, 1991, p.133) belongs to Doutai (tds, dout1240), not Duvle.

new_statements.quote: [p.19] Unlike languages of the Trans-New-Guinea Phylum in the area, tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plains languages and therefore was most likely a feature of PLP as well. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Sikaritai has only these tones and Martin (1991) analyzes the system as pitch-accent. The remainer of the languages also have combinations [p.20] of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.), and Iau, because of deleting the segments of a syllable but not the tones, has more than one tone pattern on a syllable. // [pp.12-13] The very meager word list available at this writing for Duvle is insufficient to adequately discuss the phonological changes from PT to this language.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Rendered PDF pp.8, 11, 12 of (two-page spreads = journal pp.12-13, 18-19, 20-21) and read the page images, plus the 300 dpi scanned file. Sec. 10 'Tone Typology', p.19 right column, reads exactly 'Unlike languages of the Trans-New-Guinea Phylum in the area, tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plains languages and therefore was most likely a feature of PLP as well. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Sikaritai has only these tones and Martin (1991) analyzes the system as pitch accent. The remainer of the languages also have combinations' and continues on p.20 'of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi and al…
new_statements.relation_note: Same reading as the existing Clouse 1997 statement (tone language, no stress statement), but weaker: 1993 is the precursor text written before Murdoch's phonology summary was available to Clouse, so it lacks 1997's Duvle-specific 'only high and low tone' and Appendix 3 'stress.. not contrastive' sentences. Compatible with the empty catalog record (no rule).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Duvle is covered only by the family-wide sentence: all Lakes Plains languages (Duvle is listed among them, under 'Central Lakes Plains Family', p.25) are tonal with at least high and low tone. The article never uses the word 'stress' and says nothing about Duvle prosody specifically; the Duvle section says the word list was too meager to discuss its phonology at all.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the 1993 tone section names Sikaritai alone as a two-tone (pitch accent per Martin 1991) system and does not name Duvle, unlike Clouse 1997 p.152 which adds Duvle to that group
new_statements.identity_note: Both works treat Duvle as a single language (Clouse 1993 classifies it under the Central Lakes Plains Family, p.25, after calling it an isolate within Tariku in sec.5); no dialect is specified. Ethnologue's Eastern/Western Duvle split is not addressed by either work.

sources.note: Sec. 6 'The Duvle isolate' (pp.143-145) gives Duvle syllable patterns, 10 consonants, 7 vowels, no nasals, all from Murdoch's unpublished summary ('very limited data.. a summary, which does not include examples'); no stress remark there. Sec. 11 p.152: 'All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones'. App. 3 p.160 (family-level): stress not marked, 'has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date'. p.162: Duvle word list from C. Murdoch, Nov 1992, Dagai. No statement of where stress falls in Duvle.
